name: Posture collar

card.summary: A rigid, high neck collar that holds the head upright and level, used historically and in fetish practice to enforce erect head carriage.
card.note: Not a medical device; medical cervical collars are designed for injury stabilisation.

quick.overview:
A posture collar is a stiff, tall collar, usually leather, metal or composite, that encircles the neck and limits head movement so the chin stays up and the neck stays upright. The appearance payoff is an elongated, erect neck line and head carriage while it is worn.

Today it is documented mainly within BDSM and fetish gear, though neck devices for deportment have older precedents: 19th-century accounts describe backboards that extended to the neck. No clinical studies of posture collars for forward head posture were identified.
quick.how: Wearers fasten it with buckles, lacing or locks. Heights typically run from a few inches upward, and designs may include padding and D-rings. It holds posture only while worn.
quick.risks: Rigid neck restriction can cause muscle strain or circulatory discomfort in prolonged wear, and sources on the gear stress proper sizing. Medical cervical collars are used under clinical guidance, and several small trials have led to reduced routine use, citing pressure ulcers and neck pain.

lead: A posture collar is a rigid, high-standing collar, typically leather, metal or composite, that encircles the neck and restricts forward tilt, backward extension and turning of the head, enforcing an upright head position.[1] While worn it produces a long, level neck and raised chin, which is the look wearers seek.

Contemporary use is described mainly within BDSM and fetish practice, where such collars often carry D-rings and locks; the term appears in 1980s and 1990s fetish literature.[1] Posture-shaping devices for the neck have older precedents in Victorian deportment: wooden backboards strapped behind a child's back, in some accounts extended to the neck, were worn to discourage slouching, tied to ideas of breeding and marriage prospects.[2]
Medical cervical collars are a different category, designed to immobilise suspected neck injuries, with documented risks such as pressure ulcers and neck pain.[3]

chain: Longer-looking neck and upright carriage while worn
angle.text: The collar mechanically holds the head up, giving an upright, elongated neck line while worn. Whether wearing one changes habitual posture afterward has not been studied.

paras: Stiff leather such as bridle or latigo is common, with metal-reinforced and PVC variants; fastening is by buckles, lacing or padlocks, and interior padding reduces chafing.[1]

Victorian back straighteners were wooden boards strapped behind a child, arms hooked over the ends; museum and blog accounts say they were worn through the day and criticised by doctors in the 19th century. One 19th-century description has the board extending to the neck with a leather-covered steel ring.[2]

Grokipedia's overview of the gear cautions about strain and circulatory issues in prolonged wear.[1] For medical collars, Wikipedia reports risks including raised intracranial pressure in brain injury, restricted airway access, pressure ulcers and neck pain.[3]

timeline.event: Modern medical cervical collar invented by George Cottrell.[3]
